newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: Austrian activists call for gene food referendum.
newsitem.headline: Austrian activists call for gene food referendum.

text.p: Austria's soybean stew heated up on Thursday as environmentalists vowed to seek a referendum on halting the import of genetically modified foods after a meeting with Chancellor Franz Vranitzky proved fruitless.

Pressure groups Greenpeace and Global 2000 told Reuters that a meeting with Vranitzky, Environment Minister Martin Bartenstein and Health Minister Christa Krammer brought no concessions from the government.

Austria, normally a trailblazer in environmental issues, has so far resisted calls to go it alone and slap a ban on genetically modified foods. Instead the government has chosen to back an EU agreement to label affected products.

"This is a very weak solution and totally unacceptable to environmental groups," said Florian Faber of Greenpeace Austria. He announced that the group would start a petition against genetically altered foods early next year.
If it succeeds in collecting more than 100,000 signatures, parliament will be forced to call a referendum on the issue.

A recent survey found that 80 percent of Austrians did not want to see genetically engineered products on supermarket shelves, and leading retailers Spar and Julius Meinl have already responded with their own ban.
Greens parliamentary leader Madeleine Petrovic went even further and called on Health Minister Krammer to resign.
"It would be better if the person responsible for consumer protection stepped down and left her agenda to the Spar chain," she said in a statement.
"The inability of the government to protect Austrian consumers is a sign that the population must take things into its own hands and hold a referendum," Faber said.

The first U.S. shipments of genetically modified soy were reported to have arrived in Antwerp three weeks ago, and pressure groups say derivative products such as flour and oil could already be on supermarket shelves around Europe.

Environmental pressure groups fear there could be health risks from the beans, developed by U.S. chemicals giant Monsanto Co to resist the widely used Roundup weedkiller. Soy is used in a wide range of foodstuffs, including margarine, chocolate and mayonnaise.
But the government argues there is not sufficient proof of health risks to demand a European Union ban.
"The only really adequate measure is to label products to inform the consumers and give them the choice. All other measures are absurd and naive," said Martin Mayr, advisor to the health ministry.
Austria has done an about face since March, when it voted with Sweden and Denmark against authorising the import of the so-called Roundup Ready soybeans into the European Union.

Around half of all the organic farms in the European Union are in Austria and some 10 percent of the nation's farms are devoted to organic methods. Most of the big food chains have a section marketing their own organic food line.
